newsitem.title: UK: UK Cardinal offers cash help to women not to abort.
newsitem.headline: UK Cardinal offers cash help to women not to abort.

text.p: The leader of Scotland's Roman Catholics is to offer financial help to women to convince them not to have abortions, a British newspaper reported.
Cardinal Thomas Winning is to make the offer at a conference in Glasgow organised by the anti-abortion group, the Society for the Protection of the Unborn Child, the Sunday Telegraph said.
It said the cardinal, an outspoken anti-abortion campaigner interviewed by the newspaper ahead of the conference, would say the church should "put its money where its mouth is".
But the news sparked immediate controversy with one group accusing Winning of putting unfair pressure on women.

"Nobody wants to have an abortion and the decision is only taken after much heart-searching," said Jane Rowe, a spokeswoman for the Abortion Law Reform Association which campaigns for abortion on demand in the first three months of pregnancy.
"All the church will be doing is getting women through a difficult patch and then dumping them," she told the paper.

The newspaper said the cardinal, who last October attacked opposition Labour leader Tony Blair for privately opposing abortion but publicly backing women's right to choose, would repeat that abortion could not be justified.
It said he planned to say: "If you need financial assistance or help with equipment for your baby and feel financial pressures will force you to have an abortion, we will help you

"If you cannot face your family, or if pressure in your local area is making you consider abortion, come to us, we will help you find somewhere to have your baby surrounded by support and encouragement.
"And finally, if you have had an abortion, if you are torn apart with guilt, if your relationship has split up because of abortion, if you are suffering from post-abortion stress, come to us."
The cardinal's offer was praised by anti-abortion groups.

Jack Scarisbrick, chairman of anti-abortion charity Life, said: "Of course he will be accused of bribing these women. But the plain fact of the matter is that economic considerations do weigh heavily with women facing a difficult pregnancy."

Britain passed a law permitting doctors to give abortions 30 years ago and polls show 64 percent of people now believe women should be allowed to choose whether to terminate their pregnancies, 10 percentage points more than in 1967.
